source: While now the fated Pequod had been so long afloat this voyage, the log and line had but very seldom been in use. Owing to a confident reliance upon other means of determining the vessel’s place, some merchantmen, and many whalemen, especially when cruising, wholly neglect to heave the log; though at the same time, and frequently more for form’s sake than anything else, regularly putting down upon the customary slate the course steered by the ship, as well as the presumed average rate of progression every hour. It had been thus with the Pequod. The wooden reel and angular log attached hung, long untouched, just beneath the railing of the after bulwarks. Rains and spray had damped it; sun and wind had warped it; all the elements had combined to rot a thing that hung so idly. But heedless of all this, his mood seized Ahab, as he happened to glance upon the reel, not many hours after the magnet scene, and he remembered how his quadrant was no more, and recalled his frantic oath about the level log and line. The ship was sailing plungingly; astern the billows rolled in riots.
“Forward, there! Heave the log!”
Two seamen came. The golden-hued Tahitian and the grizzly Manxman. “Take the reel, one of ye, I’ll heave.”
They went towards the extreme stern, on the ship’s lee side, where the deck, with the oblique energy of the wind, was now almost dipping into the creamy, sidelong-rushing sea.

The Manxman took the reel, and holding it high up, by the projecting handle-ends of the spindle, round which the spool of line revolved, so stood with the angular log hanging downwards, till Ahab advanced to him.

Ahab stood before him, and was lightly unwinding some thirty or forty turns to form a preliminary hand-coil to toss overboard, when the old Manxman, who was intently eyeing both him and the line, made bold to speak.
“Sir, I mistrust it; this line looks far gone, long heat and wet have spoiled it.”
“’Twill hold, old gentleman. Long heat and wet, have they spoiled thee? Thou seem’st to hold. Or, truer perhaps, life holds thee; not thou it.”
“I hold the spool, sir. But just as my captain says. With these grey hairs of mine ’tis not worth while disputing, ’specially with a superior, who’ll ne’er confess.”
“What’s that? There now’s a patched professor in Queen Nature’s granite-founded College; but methinks he’s too subservient. Where wert thou born?”
“In the little rocky Isle of Man, sir.”
“Excellent! Thou’st hit the world by that.”
“I know not, sir, but I was born there.”

“In the Isle of Man, hey? Well, the other way, it’s good. Here’s a man from Man; a man born in once independent Man, and now unmanned of Man; which is sucked in—by what? Up with the reel! The dead, blind wall butts all inquiring heads at last. Up with it! So.”

The log was heaved. The loose coils rapidly straightened out in a long dragging line astern, and then, instantly, the reel began to whirl. In turn, jerkingly raised and lowered by the rolling billows, the towing resistance of the log caused the old reelman to stagger strangely.
“Hold hard!”
Snap! the overstrained line sagged down in one long festoon; the tugging log was gone.

“I crush the quadrant, the thunder turns the needles, and now the mad sea parts the log-line. But Ahab can mend all. Haul in here, Tahitian; reel up, Manxman. And look ye, let the carpenter make another log, and mend thou the line. See to it.”

“There he goes now; to him nothing’s happened; but to me, the skewer seems loosening out of the middle of the world. Haul in, haul in, Tahitian! These lines run whole, and whirling out: come in broken, and dragging slow. Ha, Pip? come to help; eh, Pip?”

“Pip? whom call ye Pip? Pip jumped from the whale-boat. Pip’s missing. Let’s see now if ye haven’t fished him up here, fisherman. It drags hard; I guess he’s holding on. Jerk him, Tahiti! Jerk him off; we haul in no cowards here. Ho! there’s his arm just breaking water. A hatchet! a hatchet! cut it off—we haul in no cowards here. Captain Ahab! sir, sir! here’s Pip, trying to get on board again.”
“Peace, thou crazy loon,” cried the Manxman, seizing him by the arm. “Away from the quarter-deck!”
“The greater idiot ever scolds the lesser,” muttered Ahab, advancing. “Hands off from that holiness! Where sayest thou Pip was, boy?
“Astern there, sir, astern! Lo! lo!”
“And who art thou, boy? I see not my reflection in the vacant pupils of thy eyes. Oh God! that man should be a thing for immortal souls to sieve through! Who art thou, boy?”

“Bell-boy, sir; ship’s-crier; ding, dong, ding! Pip! Pip! Pip! One hundred pounds of clay reward for Pip; five feet high—looks cowardly—quickest known by that! Ding, dong, ding! Who’s seen Pip the coward?”

“There can be no hearts above the snow-line. Oh, ye frozen heavens! look down here. Ye did beget this luckless child, and have abandoned him, ye creative libertines. Here, boy; Ahab’s cabin shall be Pip’s home henceforth, while Ahab lives. Thou touchest my inmost centre, boy; thou art tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings. Come, let’s down.”

“What’s this? here’s velvet shark-skin,” intently gazing at Ahab’s hand, and feeling it. “Ah, now, had poor Pip but felt so kind a thing as this, perhaps he had ne’er been lost! This seems to me, sir, as a man-rope; something that weak souls may hold by. Oh, sir, let old Perth now come and rivet these two hands together; the black one with the white, for I will not let this go.”

“Oh, boy, nor will I thee, unless I should thereby drag thee to worse horrors than are here. Come, then, to my cabin. Lo! ye believers in gods all goodness, and in man all ill, lo you! see the omniscient gods oblivious of suffering man; and man, though idiotic, and knowing not what he does, yet full of the sweet things of love and gratitude. Come! I feel prouder leading thee by thy black hand, than though I grasped an Emperor’s!”

“There go two daft ones now,” muttered the old Manxman. “One daft with strength, the other daft with weakness. But here’s the end of the rotten line—all dripping, too. Mend it, eh? I think we had best have a new line altogether. I’ll see Mr. Stubb about it.”

modern_en.title: Chapter 125 — The Log and Line
paragraphs: Though the fated Pequod had now been afloat so long on this voyage, the log and line — a wooden float paid out astern from a reel on a line, to measure the ship's speed — had very seldom been used. Owing to a confident reliance on other means of determining the vessel's position, some merchantmen, and many whalemen, especially when cruising, wholly neglect to heave the log; though at the same time, and often more for form's sake than anything else, they regularly put down on the customary slate the course steered by the ship, as well as the presumed average rate of progress every hour. It had been so with the Pequod. The wooden reel and the angular log attached to it hung, long untouched, just beneath the railing of the after bulwarks. Rain and spray had dampened it; sun and wind had warped it; all the elements had combined to rot a thing that hung so idly. But, heedless of all this, his mood seized Ahab as he happened to glance at the reel, not many hours after the magnet scene; and he remembered that his quadrant was no more, and recalled his frantic oath about the level log and line. The ship was sailing with a plunging motion; astern, the billows rolled in riots.
"Forward, there! Heave the log!"
Two seamen came. The golden-hued Tahitian and the grizzled Manxman. "Take the reel, one of you; I'll heave."
They went toward the far end of the stern, on the ship's lee side, where the deck, tilted by the slanting force of the wind, was now almost dipping into the creamy sea that rushed past alongside.

The Manxman took the reel and held it up high by the handles sticking out at each end of the spindle on which the spool of line turned; he stood like that, with the angular log hanging down, until Ahab came up to him.

Ahab stood in front of him and was lightly unwinding some thirty or forty turns to make a preliminary hand-coil for tossing overboard, when the old Manxman, who was watching both him and the line intently, ventured to speak.
"Sir, I mistrust it; this line looks far gone. Long heat and wet have spoiled it."
"It will hold, old gentleman. Long heat and wet — have they spoiled you? You seem to hold. Or, truer perhaps, life holds you; not you it."
"I hold the spool, sir. But just as my captain says. With these gray hairs of mine, it's not worth while disputing, especially with a superior who'll never confess."
"What's that? There now's a patched professor in Queen Nature's granite-founded College; but I think he's too subservient. Where were you born?"
"In the little rocky Isle of Man, sir."
"Excellent! You've hit the world by that."
"I don't know, sir, but I was born there."

"In the Isle of Man, eh? Well, taken the other way, it's good. Here's a man from Man; a man born in once-independent Man, and now unmanned of Man; which is sucked in — by what? Up with the reel! In the end the dead, blind wall butts every questioning head. Up with it! There."

The log was heaved. The loose coils rapidly straightened out in a long dragging line astern, and then instantly the reel began to whirl. In turn, as the log was jerkingly raised and lowered by the rolling waves, its towing resistance caused the old reelman to stagger strangely.
"Hold hard!"
Snap! The line, strained too far, sagged down in a single long loop; the tugging log was gone.

"I smash the quadrant, the thunder reverses the needles, and now the mad sea snaps the log-line. But Ahab can mend everything. Haul in here, Tahitian; reel up, Manxman. And listen: get the carpenter to make another log, and you mend the line. See to it."

"There he goes now; to him nothing has happened; but to me it feels as if the skewer is working loose from the middle of the world. Haul in, haul in, Tahitian! These lines go out whole and whirling, and come back broken and dragging slow. Ha, Pip? Come to help, eh, Pip?"

"Pip? Who are you calling Pip? Pip jumped from the whale-boat. Pip's missing. Let's see now if you haven't fished him up here, fisherman. It drags hard; I guess he's holding on. Jerk him, Tahiti! Jerk him off; we haul in no cowards here. Ho! There's his arm just breaking water. A hatchet! A hatchet! Cut it off — we haul in no cowards here. Captain Ahab! Sir, sir! Here's Pip, trying to get on board again."

"Astern there, sir, astern! Look! Look!"

"Bell-boy, sir; ship's crier; ding, dong, ding! Pip! Pip! Pip! One hundred pounds of clay reward for Pip; five feet high — looks cowardly — quickest known by that! Ding, dong, ding! Who's seen Pip the coward?"

"There can be no hearts above the snow-line. Oh, you frozen heavens! Look down here. You begot this luckless child, and have abandoned him, you creative libertines. Here, boy; Ahab's cabin shall be Pip's home henceforth, while Ahab lives. You touch my inmost center, boy; you are tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings. Come, let's go down."

This seems to me, sir, like a man-rope, something weak souls can hold on to. Oh, sir, let old Perth come now and rivet these two hands together, the black one with the white, for I won't let this go."

"Oh, boy, nor will I let go of you, unless by holding on I should drag you to worse horrors than are here. Come, then, to my cabin. Look, you believers in gods all goodness and in man all ill — look, you! See the omniscient gods oblivious of suffering man; and man, though idiotic and not knowing what he does, yet full of the sweet things of love and gratitude. Come! I feel prouder leading you by your black hand than if I grasped an Emperor's!"

modern_da.title: Kapitel 125 — Loggen og linen
paragraphs: Selv om det dømte Pequod nu havde været så længe til søs på denne rejse, var logglinen — et stykke træ, der bliver firet ud agterude fra en rulle på en line for at måle skibets fart — kun meget sjældent blevet brugt. På grund af en sikker tillid til andre midler til at bestemme skibets position forsømmer nogle handelsskibe og mange hvalfangere, især når de krydser, helt at kaste loggen. Til gengæld skriver de, ofte mere for formens skyld end af anden grund, regelmæssigt den kurs, skibet har styret, på den sædvanlige tavle, samt den formodede gennemsnitlige fart hver time. Sådan havde det været med Pequod. Trærullen og den kantede log, der var fastgjort til den, havde hængt længe urørt lige under rælingen på det agterste skansekled. Regn og stænk havde gjort den fugtig; sol og vind havde fået den til at slå sig; alle elementerne havde forenet sig om at rådne en ting, der hang så ledigt. Men uden at bekymre sig om alt dette blev Ahab grebet af sit lune, da han tilfældigvis kastede et blik på rullen, ikke mange timer efter magnetscenen; og han huskede, at hans kvadrant var ødelagt, og mindedes sin vilde ed om den vandrette log og line. Skibet sejlede med en stampende bevægelse; agterude rullede bølgerne i oprør.
»Forude, dér! Kast loggen!«
To sømænd kom. Den gyldenfarvede tahitianer og den gråsprængte manxmand. »Tag rullen, en af jer; jeg kaster.«

De gik hen mod den fjerneste ende af agterstavnen, på skibets le side, hvor dækket, der var skråtstillet af vindens skrå kraft, nu næsten dyppede ned i det flødeskummende hav, der strømmede forbi langs siden.

Manxmanden tog rullen og holdt den højt oppe i de håndtag, der stak ud i hver ende af den spindel, som linespolen drejede sig om. Sådan stod han med den kantede log hængende ned, indtil Ahab kom hen til ham.

Ahab stillede sig foran ham og var i gang med let at rulle tredive eller fyrre vindinger af for at lave en første kveil i hånden til at kaste over bord, da den gamle manxmand, som holdt skarpt øje med både ham og linen, vovede at tale.
»Sir, jeg stoler ikke på den; linen ser ud til at være helt færdig. Lang tids hede og væde har ødelagt den.«
»Den holder, gamle mand. Lang tids hede og væde — har de ødelagt dig? Du ser ud til at holde. Eller rettere, måske: livet holder dig; ikke du det.«
»Jeg holder spolen, sir. Men det er, som min kaptajn siger. Med disse grå hår er det ikke umagen værd at skændes, i hvert fald ikke med en overordnet, der aldrig vil give sig.«
»Hvad er det? Dér har vi en lappet professor på Dronning Naturs granitgrundlagte universitet; men jeg synes, han er for underdanig. Hvor er du født?«
»På den lille klippefyldte Isle of Man, sir.«
»Fremragende! Dér har du ramt verden.«
»Det ved jeg ikke, sir, men født er jeg der.«

»På Isle of Man, ja? Nå, tager man det den anden vej, er det godt. Her er en mand fra Man; en mand født på det engang selvstændige Man og nu afmandet af Man; som bliver suget ind — af hvad? Op med rullen! Til sidst støder den døde, blinde mur panden på ethvert spørgende hoved. Op med den! Sådan.«

Loggen blev kastet ud. De løse vindinger rettede sig hurtigt ud til en lang slæbende line agter, og så begyndte rullen straks at snurre. Efterhånden som loggen blev hevet op og ned i ryk af de rullende bølger, fik dens modstand i slæbet den gamle rullemand til at rave besynderligt.
»Hold fast!«
Knæk! Linen, der var blevet strakt for langt, sank ned i én lang bugt; den trækkende log var væk.

»Jeg smadrer kvadranten, tordenen vender nålene om, og nu knækker det gale hav loglinen. Men Ahab kan reparere alt. Hal ind her, tahitianer; rul op, manxmand. Og hør: få tømreren til at lave en ny log, og du reparerer linen. Sørg for det.«

»Der går han nu; for ham er der ikke sket noget; men for mig føles det, som om tappen er ved at løsne sig midt i verden. Hal ind, hal ind, tahitianer! Disse liner går ud hele og snurrende og kommer tilbage knækkede og slæbende langsomt. Ha, Pip? Kommer du for at hjælpe, hva', Pip?«

»Pip? Hvem kalder du Pip? Pip sprang fra hvalbåden. Pip er savnet. Lad os se, om du ikke har fisket ham op her, fisker. Det trækker hårdt; jeg tror, han holder fast. Ryk ham, Tahiti! Ryk ham af; vi hiver ingen kryster ind her. Ho! Dér er hans arm lige ved at bryde vandfladen. En økse! En økse! Hug den af — vi hiver ingen kryster ind her. Kaptajn Ahab! Sir, sir! Her er Pip, som prøver at komme om bord igen.«
»Fred, din skøre tåbe,« råbte manxmanden og greb ham i armen. »Væk fra agterdækket!«
»Den største tåbe skælder altid ud på den mindre,« mumlede Ahab og trådte frem. »Hænderne væk fra den hellige! Hvor sagde du, Pip var, dreng?«
»Agterude, sir, agterude! Se! Se!«
»Og hvem er du, dreng? Jeg ser ikke mit spejlbillede i dine tomme pupiller. Åh Gud! At mennesket skal være en ting, som udødelige sjæle kan sigte sig igennem! Hvem er du, dreng?«

»Klokkedreng, sir; skibsudråber; ding, dong, ding! Pip! Pip! Pip! Hundrede pund ler i belønning for Pip; fem fod høj — ser fej ud — kendes lettest på det! Ding, dong, ding! Hvem har set Pip, krysteren?«

»Der kan ikke findes hjerter oven for snegrænsen. Åh, I frosne himle! Se herned. I avlede dette uheldige barn og har forladt ham, I skabende libertinere. Kom, dreng; Ahabs kahyt skal være Pips hjem fra nu af, så længe Ahab lever. Du rører mit inderste, dreng; du er bundet til mig med snore, flettet af mine hjertestrenge. Kom, lad os gå ned.«

»Hvad er det her? Her er fløjlshajskind,« sagde han og stirrede ihærdigt på Ahabs hånd og følte på den. »Ah, hvis stakkels Pip bare havde følt noget så venligt som det her, var han måske aldrig gået tabt! Det her forekommer mig, sir, som et rælingsreb, noget svage sjæle kan holde fast i. Åh, sir, lad gamle Perth komme nu og nitte disse to hænder sammen, den sorte med den hvide, for jeg vil ikke slippe den her.«

»Åh, dreng, og jeg slipper heller ikke dig, medmindre jeg ved at holde fast skulle trække dig ud i værre rædsler end dem, der er her. Kom så til min kahyt. Se, I, der tror på guder, som er helt gode, og på mennesker, som er helt onde — se, I! Se de alvidende guder, der ikke ænser det lidende menneske; og mennesket, der, selv om det er åndssvagt og ikke ved, hvad det gør, dog er fuldt af kærlighedens og taknemmelighedens bløde ting. Kom! Jeg føler mig stoltere ved at føre dig ved din sorte hånd, end hvis jeg holdt en kejsers!«

»Dér går to tossede,« mumlede den gamle manxmand. »Den ene tosset af styrke, den anden tosset af svaghed. Men her er enden af den rådne line — drivende våd også. Reparere den, ja? Jeg tror, vi må have en helt ny line. Jeg skal tale med Mr. Stubb om det.«
